urban.text: Water conservation systems and a rice-growing landscape connect coordinated work with urban life.

evidence.text: Urban works, differentiated burials and jade preserve different aspects of social organization; the selected cong is not tied to a city findspot.

coordination.text: Rice cultivation, earthworks and channels involved coordinated activity; archaeological hierarchy does not identify exact household obligations or recruitment arrangements.

name: Liangzhu: waterworks, rice and jade
place: Lower Yangtze region near Hangzhou, China
geographicPrecision: Archaeological city region. The cong is not assigned a findspot at this city.

interval.label: c. 3300–2300 BCE
interval.note: UNESCO’s city/site range. The Met’s broader Liangzhu culture label c3200–2000 BCE has a different scope.

question: How can waterworks and burials tell different parts of a story?
summary: Liangzhu’s rice-growing communities changed a wet landscape with dams, channels and earthen construction. Water control supported production and movement, while elaborate burials and jade reveal unequal status. These are related ways into the city’s history, with different kinds of evidence behind each. Neither a dam nor the selected cong gives a direct account of the decisions, household labor or beliefs of every resident.

sections.title: The city belonged to a wider landscape
sections.text: The archaeological property includes high dams near valley mouths, low dams on the plain, the city and Yaoshan. Rice cultivation supported this regional society. The city’s earthen monuments and differentiated cemeteries put authority and belief into the landscape alongside farming. Looking beyond the urban centre matters: a large built place depended on work and resources beyond its monumental core. The UNESCO frame of c. 3300–2300 BCE describes a site sequence, rather than the life of one unchanging government.

citations.locator: Description; Brief synthesis and property components

sections.title: Engineering involved materials and repeated work
sections.text: Excavators identified clay wrapped in grass bundles within dams. Such construction turns a general claim about coordination into a material question: people gathered, carried and placed things. Channels and controlled access points also helped move people and materials. The conceptual diagram identifies storage, channels and productive activity without supplying a traced ancient canal route. Building and maintaining a system would have had to coexist with agricultural work; the paper’s proposed labor totals are estimates based on assumptions, not surviving attendance lists.

citations.locator: Defining the Hydraulic Landscape; construction and labor assumptions

sections.title: Jade gives another view of work and status
sections.text: The selected nephrite cong has a round opening inside a squared, tapering outer form. Faces occupy its corners. Close carving and finishing made it a demanding object to produce; the Met proposes associations with wealth and status while leaving its exact meaning uncertain. Differentiated burials provide contextual evidence of social hierarchy at the archaeological property. This museum object, however, has no documented findspot at the city in the record used here. It illustrates a cultural form, not a particular excavated burial.

sections.title: Several clocks run through the same story
sections.text: The jade is catalogued around 2400 BCE, within a broader museum culture range that differs from the site’s range. Dam samples have their own radiocarbon distributions. Treating these dates as separate evidence makes it possible to ask what was built earlier, what was modified and what coexisted. It prevents a display from turning all Liangzhu works into one instant or using a late object as a photograph of an earlier construction project.

returnPrompt: Which evidence would help distinguish organizing a useful water system from controlling who benefited from it?

deeperReading.title: Coordination does not name the agreement
deeperReading.text: Earthen construction and rice production establish substantial practical tasks. Burial differences add evidence that people did not hold identical social positions. Together they support an inquiry into political organization; they do not preserve the exact relationships between leaders, specialists and households. Nor does a water-control system alone prove one universal form of coercive government. A next investigation should test how benefits, burdens and access varied, rather than treating the finished dam as an explanation of its own labor arrangements. Household and gender histories need more direct evidence than this bounded set currently supplies.

citations.locator: Conclusion: limits on reconstructing social categories

deeperReading.title: A correction changes what can be repeated
deeperReading.text: The original paper’s online body still contains superseded reservoir capacities. The 2018 correction gives about 14.98 and 50.72 million cubic metres for the high and low reservoirs respectively. These are reconstructed capacities, not measured annual water consumption or a count of people served. The source and its correction must travel together. This example shows why a visually impressive number is not enough: establish its units, whether it is a measurement or estimate, and whether later corrections change it before using it in an explanation.

familyActivity.title: Follow materials, then ask about people
steps: In the diagram, find grass-wrapped clay, water storage and rice production. Say which is a material, a structure or an activity.
Look at the cong photograph. Describe its opening and corners before reading the proposed meaning.
Choose one question the objects cannot answer directly: who gave an order, who carried clay, or how a household used its share of food.
familyActivity.explanation: The diagram is a modern concept guide, not a surveyed plan or a picture of an ancient workday. Shape and material can be observed; beliefs and social relationships need contextual evidence.

evidenceReading.title: Material evidence, dated samples and estimates
evidenceReading.introduction: The following paraphrases distinguish what was found from what a modern analysis infers.

items.label: A dated material is not the whole city
items.text: The paper dates short-lived plants and charcoal associated with dams; it reports different clusters for high and low dams.
items.interpretation: The source uses calibrated years BP, with 1950 as present. Approximate BCE equivalents are orientation aids, not new exact dates for each structure or for every phase of the city.

items.label: Read the corrected capacity
items.text: The correction replaces the high/low reservoir estimates with about 14.98/50.72 million cubic metres.
items.interpretation: The two figures describe reconstructed storage capacities. They must not be repeated as excavated grain volumes, population counts or annual water use.

items.label: A cong is not a decoded belief system
items.text: The museum identifies nephrite, a squared tube and carved faces, but describes the object’s meaning as uncertain.
items.interpretation: The city’s burials offer evidence for differentiation. They do not establish this particular object’s burial context or a certain translation of its motifs.

review.scope: Bounded early-city teaching account with main/deeper reading, source interpretation, reference chronology and an original explanatory diagram.
limitations: Dam functions and labor arrangements involve archaeological interpretation; no precise household social categories are reconstructed.
